articles.title: Before authentication: three bugs in Mullvad's gotatun
articles.excerpt: WireGuard is known for staying silent towards packets it can't authenticate. But a userspace implementation has to receive a UDP datagram before it can decide whether to ignore it. That receive path i…
articles.body: WireGuard is known for staying silent towards packets it can't authenticate. But a userspace implementation has to receive a UDP datagram before it can decide whether to ignore it. That receive path is attack surface too. I found three bugs there in gotatun , Mullvad's userspace WireGuard implementation in Rust. All three trigger before WireGuard authentication, and all three are fixed. 1. An empty datagram kills the Linux receive task GHSA-6gxq-8xp9-742r · High (CVSS 7.5) · fixed in 0.10.1 On Linux, gotatun receives datagrams in batches with recvmmsg . For each result it took the payload like this: result .iovs () .next () .expect ( "we create exactly one IoSlice" ) For an empty datagram, the iterator returns None , and expect panics.

articles.title: Two ways to stall quinn, Rust's QUIC library
articles.excerpt: quinn is a popular QUIC implementation in Rust. I reported two denial-of-service bugs to the maintainers, both are fixed. One lives in the UDP layer below QUIC, the other in how quinn handles a peer's…
articles.body: quinn is a popular QUIC implementation in Rust. I reported two denial-of-service bugs to the maintainers, both are fixed. One lives in the UDP layer below QUIC, the other in how quinn handles a peer's transport parameters. 1. recv_single() spins after a truncated datagram GHSA-6pp4-4cxf-xf88 · High · quinn-udp, fixed in 0.5.16 and 0.6.3 recv_single is the Unix fallback that receives one datagram per recvmsg call. It is used on OpenBSD and some other Unix and Apple configurations. The normal Linux batched path and Windows use different code. Two details combined into a loop: The code checked the MSG_TRUNC flag before checking whether recvmsg had failed. The msghdr was initialized only once, so its flags survived from one call to the next.

articles.title: We Open-Sourced tritify: Deterministic AI Inference with Exact Integer Arithmetic
articles.excerpt: We just open-sourced tritify — Pelloran’s deterministic AI inference runtime built around exact integer arithmetic. The core idea is simple: Same weights. Same input. Same execution schedule. Same bit…
articles.body: We just open-sourced tritify — Pelloran’s deterministic AI inference runtime built around exact integer arithmetic. The core idea is simple: Same weights. Same input. Same execution schedule. Same bits. Why this matters Typical optimized floating-point inference is not bit-identical across environments by default. Different hardware, compiler behavior, reduction order, threading, or math libraries can change the low-order bits of a result. For many workloads, that is acceptable. But if you want AI inference to be independently reproducible and verifiable, “almost the same” is not the same as “the same.” tritify takes a different approach. Its runtime inference path uses fully specified integer arithmetic so that the output can be reproduced exactly across supported environments.
articles.author: Pelloran

articles.body: Follow one failed checkout from the browser to the dependency, so every debugging step gives you a reason for the next one. Your customer has clicked Pay twice, and you are staring at a Kubernetes dashboard that seems delighted with itself. Every pod is Running, readiness checks are green, and CPU usage looks ordinary. Meanwhile, checkout still fails, which makes all that reassuring green feel a little less reassuring. Honestly, this is the kind of debugging exercise I want in my practice notes because it exposes a very tempting assumption. A process can answer its health check while the operation a customer needs is broken. Let’s work through a hypothetical checkout failure and use one request to decide where to look next.

articles.title: The A2A CLI on AWS: One Client for Lightsail, Bedrock AgentCore and Localhost
articles.excerpt: The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) CLI solves a specific problem: you want to run the same agent code on your laptop, in a Lightsail container, and inside Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, then call them all with iden…
articles.body: The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) CLI solves a specific problem: you want to run the same agent code on your laptop, in a Lightsail container, and inside Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, then call them all with identical commands. The CLI handles authentication, protocol version mismatches, and cross-environment routing so you can test locally and deploy without rewriting your orchestration layer. This is not a managed service. It is a command-line client that speaks A2A protocol versions 0.3 and 1.0, carries agent-to-agent calls between environments, and abstracts the differences between localhost HTTP, Lightsail public endpoints, and Bedrock AgentCore's Cognito-gated runtime.

articles.title: Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long
articles.excerpt: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and QQ8 is sticking around for Christmas.
articles.body: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas. The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29). The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027. Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun . QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Almathea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft flew by a small moon called Amalthea and made a surprising find. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists. The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft. The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong.

articles.title: You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters
articles.excerpt: After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.
articles.body: TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection. Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it. "The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 probe bounces back from communications glitch in interstellar space
articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is back in communication after the 49-year-old spacecraft briefly fell silent last month, during its interstellar-space mission.
articles.body: Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month. The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix. "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.
